title: Bellman-Ford algorithm: negative weights, cycle detection, Python code — cv.cm
description: Bellman-Ford explained: shortest paths with negative edge weights, a traced example, Python code, negative cycle detection and O(V × E) time complexity.
h1: Bellman-Ford algorithm explained: how it works, code and complexity
answer: The Bellman-Ford algorithm finds the shortest paths from one start node to all other nodes, even when some edge weights are negative. It relaxes every edge V − 1 times; after that, all shortest distances are correct. One extra pass detects a negative cycle: if any distance can still be improved, the graph has a cycle with negative total weight. It runs in O(V × E) time.

body: Dijkstra's algorithm is fast but requires non-negative edge weights. Some problems naturally have negative weights: a refund, a gain in a currency exchange, or an energy cost that can go below zero. Bellman-Ford handles these graphs correctly and also tells you when no shortest path exists because of a negative cycle, a loop you could go around forever to make the cost smaller and smaller.
The algorithm is named after Richard Bellman and Lester Ford Jr., who published versions of it in the 1950s.

ol: Set the distance of the start node to 0 and all others to infinity.
Repeat V − 1 times: for every edge u → v with weight w, if `dist[u] + w < dist[v]`, update `dist[v]`.
Do one more pass over all edges. If any distance still improves, report a negative cycle.

body: Why V − 1 rounds? A shortest path without cycles uses at most V − 1 edges. After round k, every node whose shortest path has at most k edges already has its correct distance, so V − 1 rounds cover every simple path.
Directed graph with 4 nodes and the edges S→A (4), S→B (5), B→A (−3), A→C (3). The edges are processed in this order in every round.

In round 1, A first becomes 4 through S→A, then improves to 2 through B→A, and C uses the improved value. Dijkstra's algorithm would finalize A at 4 before looking at B, which is exactly the mistake a negative edge causes.

The `dist[u] != INF` check skips edges that leave nodes not reached yet. In Python, `float("inf") + w` is still infinity, so the check mainly saves work. In languages that use a large integer as infinity, it prevents overflow and false updates.

body: On a graph with 1,000 nodes and 10,000 edges that is up to about 10 million relaxations, so Dijkstra is much faster when all weights are non-negative.

ul: Early exit: stop when a full round changes nothing. This is safe and often makes the algorithm much faster in practice.
SPFA (shortest path faster algorithm): only re-relax edges out of nodes whose distance changed, using a queue. It is often fast but has the same O(V × E) worst case.
Hop-limited paths: running exactly k rounds, using a copy of the distances from the previous round, gives the cheapest path with at most k edges. This solves "cheapest flights within k stops".
Finding the cycle itself: keep a parent map; when the extra pass updates node v, follow parents V times to land inside the cycle, then walk until you return to the same node.

body.note: A negative cycle only matters if it is reachable from the start. A cycle in a part of the graph you cannot reach does not affect the distances, and the `dist[u] != INF` guard correctly ignores it. In an undirected graph, any negative edge is itself a negative cycle (go back and forth), so Bellman-Ford is mainly used on directed graphs.

sections.h: When to use it and real-world uses

ul: Use Bellman-Ford when edge weights can be negative or when you must detect negative cycles. Otherwise prefer Dijkstra.
Distance-vector routing protocols, such as RIP, use the distributed Bellman-Ford idea: each router repeatedly updates its distance estimates from its neighbors' estimates.
Currency arbitrage: with weights equal to `-log(rate)`, a negative cycle is a sequence of exchanges that ends with more money than it started with.
Johnson's algorithm runs Bellman-Ford once to re-weight a graph so that Dijkstra can then be used from every node for all-pairs shortest paths.
Difference constraints (systems of inequalities like `x - y <= c`) can be solved as shortest paths; a negative cycle means no solution exists.

faq.q: Why does Bellman-Ford run V − 1 iterations?
faq.a: A shortest path without cycles contains at most V − 1 edges, and each round fixes the distances of paths with one more edge. After V − 1 rounds every shortest path is found, unless there is a negative cycle.

faq.q: How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative cycle?
faq.a: It does one more pass over all edges after the V − 1 rounds. If any distance can still be reduced, some path keeps getting cheaper, which is only possible with a reachable negative cycle.
No. Bellman-Ford is O(V × E), while Dijkstra with a heap is O((V + E) log V). Use Bellman-Ford only when you need negative weights or cycle detection.
